name: Aaron Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Aaron. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to companies, unions or parties, and this is all confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage an eight-person analytics team in the online shopping side of a big supermarket chain. We work out which offers to send to which customers, why basket sizes dropped in a region, that sort of thing. My mornings are dashboards and my afternoons are meetings with the marketing people who want the numbers to say something they don't.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzles, and I like that I've got the team using AI every day now. I wrote a set of scripts that builds our Monday report automatically, which used to take two people a full day. What wears me out is presenting to directors who skim the first slide and decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I tell people already, that it's a good tool if you know how to use it. On LinkedIn I'd probably write a short post about using AI for the boring bits and keeping humans for judgement. At work I'd just keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it suits me fine. I'm already ahead of most people on the AI tools, and if they plateau, that lead lasts longer. My job is safe and my pay is normal for the role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate a few more reports, and push the team to spend the saved time on actual analysis. I'd keep putting money into an index fund every month, which I started last year. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Probably a little bored, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Bored? You'd miss the change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I like being early to things, and this picture says there's not much to be early to. I'd find another hobby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anyone on your team who'd feel even this small change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe Bilal, our most junior analyst, because most of his week is pulling data the scripts already pull. I'd want to teach him the modelling side so he isn't the one people point at.

say: AI is **a good tool** if you know how to use it.
I'd post about using AI for **the boring bits** and humans for judgement.
think: I'm **ahead on the tools**, so a plateau keeps my lead longer.
My job is **safe** and my pay is normal.
do: Keep putting money into an **index fund** every month.
S0.quote: I'm already ahead of most people on the AI tools, and if they plateau, that lead lasts longer.
fieldNote: Feels **secure** and slightly bored by a world without much change.
Protective of **Bilal**, whose data-pulling work shrinks first.

steps.text: Automate two more weekly reports for the team
Keep the monthly index fund payment going
Train Bilal on modelling so his role grows

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where you see who adapts, and I'd mean it kindly. At work I'd say we should be the team that shows how it's done, not the one it's done to. I'd write about it online, practical stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think analytics teams shrink a lot. My eight becomes maybe four, but I'm the one who sets up the tools, so I'd probably stay. I'm a bit uneasy about who the four are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate as much of our routine reporting as I can, this quarter, and use it to argue for keeping the team on harder questions. I'd do a proper course in machine learning in the evenings. And I'd start some weekend consulting for small shops wanting the same setup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more interested than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Aren't you the one automating your own team away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair. It's both, honestly. If I don't do it, someone in head office does it worse and cuts deeper. I'd rather be in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Noor, your partner, say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor would say watch you don't get too pleased with yourself. She teaches seven-year-olds, and she thinks I underestimate how fast things change. She's usually right.

say: This is where you see **who adapts**, and I mean that kindly.
We should show how it's done, **not be done to**.
think: Analytics teams **shrink a lot**, maybe eight to four.
I'd likely **stay** because I set up the tools.
do: **Automate** routine reporting this quarter to free the team for harder questions.
S1.quote: We should be the team that shows how it's done, not the one it's done to.
fieldNote: Expects his **own job** to survive as the tool builder.
Admits he would be **shrinking his own team**, and justifies it pragmatically.

steps.text: Automate the team's routine reporting this quarter
Take an evening machine learning course
Offer weekend analytics setups to small local shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and we need to be honest about it, no spin. At work I'd tell the team straight that analytics as a job is in trouble. Online I'd share what I'm doing, in case it helps someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, being good with AI doesn't help if AI doesn't need me. In two years it does what my team does and what I do, including setting up the tools. So my job goes, and fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut costs straight away and put more into cash, not the index fund. I'd go hard on the consulting side, helping small businesses use the tools while they still need a person to set it up. And I'd look at jobs in companies that put AI into warehouses and stores, because the robots are three years behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the first time I'd feel my skills don't matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the consulting a real income or a stopgap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. For a year, maybe, small businesses would pay someone to set it up. After that, the AI sets itself up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's steadiest at home in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor's job, weirdly. Teaching young kids is hands-on and human, and parents won't hand that over in two years. So she'd be steadier than me, which is a strange thing to say.

say: This is **huge**, and we need honesty about it, not spin.
Analytics as a job is **in trouble**.
think: Being good with AI doesn't help if **AI doesn't need me**.
My job goes **fast**, including setting up the tools.
do: Cut costs and move savings into **cash**.
Go hard on **consulting** for small businesses for a year.
Apply to firms putting AI into **warehouses and stores**.
feel: **Alarmed**; the first time his **skills** feel irrelevant.
S2.quote: Being good with AI doesn't help if AI doesn't need me.
fieldNote: His **adaptability** stops protecting him when AGI comes in two years.
Sees consulting as a **stopgap**, not a career.
Notes partner Noor's **teaching** job is steadier than his.

steps.text: Pause the index fund and hold savings in cash
Sell AI setup work to small businesses for a year
Apply to firms putting robots into warehouses and stores

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight, but enough to move if you start now. I'd say that on LinkedIn and I'd say it to my team. I'd want the company to fund training for anyone who wants it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my current job ends around 2031. But five years lets me build something on the side and move into the physical side of AI before robots arrive in 2034. I'd be thirty-two with five years of AI rollouts on my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for every AI project at the supermarket, especially the ones in stores and warehouses. I'd build up the weekend consulting into something real. And I'd keep saving, with half in cash and half in the index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in an energetic way. Lots to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're betting on AI again. Is that wise when AI is what takes your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might be, yes. But I'd rather bet on something I'm good at than run to something I'm not. If it goes wrong by year three, I'd still have savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team to start learning now, all of them, not just the keen ones. Bilal especially. I'd spend team time on it, even if directors complained.

say: Five years is **tight but enough** if you start now.
The company should fund **training** for anyone who wants it.
think: I can move into the **physical side** of AI before robots arrive in 2034.
do: Volunteer for every store and **warehouse** AI project at the supermarket.
Grow the weekend **consulting** into a real business.
Split savings between **cash** and the index fund.
S3.quote: I'd rather bet on something I'm good at than run to something I'm not.
fieldNote: Still expects his **current job** to end, but uses five years to reposition.
Aims at the **physical rollout** of AI, timing it to the robot gap.
Wants his whole team, including **Bilal**, trained now.

steps.text: Volunteer for the supermarket's store and warehouse AI projects
Turn the weekend consulting into a registered business
Keep saving, half in cash and half in the index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a proper runway, so let's not waste it arguing. At work I'd push for a long training plan. Online I'd be fairly upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. I'd spend the decade building AI into the supermarket and then into stores and warehouses, and by 2036 I'd have a career in the change itself. At thirty-seven that's a good spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and push further into AI projects. I'd keep the index fund going and maybe buy a flat with Noor in a year or two. I'd keep the consulting as a hobby, not a lifeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a little. Mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep picking jobs that AI eventually takes. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I know it. Every job I'd move into ends too, eventually, but ten years is long enough to move twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bilal, and people like him. Ten years is a long time to stay ahead if you're junior and nobody trains you. I'd want the company to fund it, not leave it to luck.

say: Ten years is **a proper runway**, so let's not waste it.
I'd push for a **long training plan** at work.
think: I'd be **fine**, with a career built around the change itself.
At **thirty-seven** that's a good spot to be in.
do: Push further into **AI projects** at the supermarket.
Keep the **index fund** going and buy a flat with Noor.
Keep consulting as a **hobby**, not a lifeline.
S4.quote: Every job I'd move into ends too, eventually, but ten years is long enough to move twice.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his **adaptability** back into an edge over most colleagues.
Honest that his **target jobs** also end eventually.
Concern shifts to **junior staff** without training.

steps.text: Lead more of the supermarket's AI projects
Buy a flat with Noor within two years
Keep the current analytics job while building experience

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's the one where being good with the tools stops mattering. What would help is notice, and a bit of breathing room, like government support for people moving into new kinds of work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how the people who adapt feel. We're supposed to be the winners. But a lot of us early adopters are just running slightly ahead of the same wave.

headlineQuote: A lot of us early adopters are just running slightly ahead of the same wave.
portrait: Aaron, 27, manages **eight analysts** at a supermarket's online division and lives with Noor, a teacher.
He uses AI **every day** and has already automated his team's Monday report.
Pragmatic and centrist, he thinks it's better to be **in the room** than resist.
He is calm or uneasy in slower pictures, but **alarmed** when AGI arrives in two years.
He bets on the **physical rollout** of AI and admits his target jobs end too.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, where being good with **the tools** stops mattering.
whatWouldHelp: Government support for moving into **new kinds of work**.
